title: Maximum likelihood for autoregressive models
blurb: Likelihood decomposition, gradient ascent, conditional models

hook.title: A thousand small dials
hook.text: An autoregressive model is a control panel of dials, one small network per conditional. To train it, show it a real image and add up how likely it finds **every pixel given the earlier ones**. Do this for all images and the total (in logs) is the log-likelihood. There's no formula for the best dial settings, so you *feel the slope* of the total and twist every dial a little uphill: gradient **ascent** on the log-likelihood (backprop does the arithmetic).
hook.recall: Remember the dials: the objective is a sum over images *and* pixels of log-conditionals; no closed form, so twist uphill by gradient ascent. High likelihood doesn't automatically mean pretty samples.

explore.intro: A tiny 3-pixel autoregressive model with 7 tabular conditionals, trained by gradient ascent on 12 images.
tasks: Press *25 steps* a few times. Do the learned probabilities approach the data frequencies?
Raise the learning rate to 3. What happens to the log-likelihood curve?

items: Repeat until the likelihood stops improving
build.explanation: Slide 37's algorithm is steps 1–3; repetition is the loop around them.

questions.prompt: For an autoregressive model, $\log L(\theta,D)$ equals:
options: $\sum_j\sum_i\log p_{neural}(x_i^{(j)}|x_{<i}^{(j)};\theta_i)$
$\prod_j\prod_ip(x_i^{(j)})$
$\log m$
questions.explanation: Log turns the product over images and pixels into a double sum of small log-conditionals: the dials.

questions.prompt: *“I train with $\theta_{t+1}=\theta_t-\alpha\nabla_\theta\ell(\theta)$ where $\ell$ is the log-likelihood.”* The error is:
options: None
$\ell$ is to be **maximised**, so the update should be $+\alpha\nabla\ell$ (or minimise $-\ell$)
$\alpha$ must be negative
Backprop can’t compute $\nabla\ell$
questions.explanation: Uphill, not downhill: we want the *highest* total likelihood.

questions.prompt: $m=1000$ binary images of $784$ pixels each. How many log-conditional terms appear in $\ell(\theta)$?
questions.explanation: One term per image per pixel: $1000\times784=784{,}000$.

questions.prompt: Which statement from the recap is correct?
options: Higher log-likelihood always means better-looking samples
Higher log-likelihood doesn’t necessarily mean better-looking samples
Likelihood can’t be computed for autoregressive models
Autoregressive models can’t be trained by MLE
questions.explanation: The dial settings that maximise total surprise-minimisation aren’t guaranteed to produce the prettiest pictures.

questions.prompt: Which statement about autoregressive models is FALSE?
options: It is easy to compute $p_\theta(x)$
Ideally each conditional is evaluated in parallel (unlike RNNs)
They are natural to train via maximum likelihood
Maximising likelihood guarantees the best-looking samples
questions.explanation: See the last recap bullet: other measures (e.g. GANs) exist.

questions.prompt: In a conditional generative model $p(y|x)$ (e.g. text-to-speech) the loss is:
options: $-\log p_\theta(y\mid x)$ and it suffices to estimate the conditional
$-\log p_\theta(x,y)$ and we must model the joint
$\|x-y\|^2$ only
$D(p_{data}(x)\|p_\theta(y))$
questions.explanation: Only the conditional matters, as the dial panel only needs to model $y$ given $x$.
